This notebook isolates the natural-gas-to-heat-pump bill-change analysis so it can run
against this batch today. `analysis.qmd` also compares MD BGE's `default` schedule to
calibrated `hp_seasonal_*`/`hp_flat_*` reform tariffs, but this batch (`md_20260909_a`) has
only run `default_r_uncalibrated` and `default_rd_uncalibrated` so far — no reform scenario
exists yet to compare against. Rather than let those missing scenarios break the whole
notebook, this one covers just the piece that *is* available: how a BGE Schedule R
customer's bill changes when they switch from natural gas to a heat pump, under the rate
exactly as filed.

The functions doing the actual data crunching are the same ones `analysis.qmd` uses, from
[`lib/rates_analysis/rate_case_funcs.py`](../../../lib/rates_analysis/rate_case_funcs.py) —
this notebook just calls a smaller subset of them, scoped to the one scenario this batch has.

## Setup

```{python}
#| label: setup

from __future__ import annotations

from pathlib import Path
from typing import cast

import polars as pl
import yaml

from lib.rates_analysis.rate_case_funcs import (
    bill_change_incidence,
    bill_delta_between_segments,
    load_master_bills,
    plot_bill_change_quadrants,
    plot_weighted_bill_change_hist,
    segment_name,
)

report_vars: dict = {}
```

## Parameters

Batch identity lives in `batch_config.yaml` alongside this report, not hardcoded here, so
re-running against a new batch is a one-file change. `BASELINE_BILL_SCENARIO` is
`"default_r_uncalibrated"` — BGE's Schedule R billed exactly as filed (CAIRO's "uncalibrated"
mode, meaning the tariff itself isn't recalibrated to hit a revenue-requirement target; see
`pipeline_bge.yaml`'s comment: "Posted Schedule R billed as-is"). That's a different
"calibrated" than the *stage* name below — don't confuse the two.

```{python}
#| label: params

_batch_config = yaml.safe_load(Path("../batch_config.yaml").read_text())

STATE = _batch_config["STATE"]
BATCH = _batch_config["BATCH"]
UTILITY = "bge"

# bills
BILL_COL_LMI_CURRENT = "energy_total_bill_lmi_48"
BILL_COL_LMI_100 = "energy_total_bill_lmi_100"
BILL_COL_BASELINE = "energy_total_bill"

# this is the column that will be used for all comparisons and plots
BILL_COL = BILL_COL_BASELINE  # BILL_COL_BASELINE, BILL_COL_LMI_CURRENT, or BILL_COL_LMI_100

DEFAULT_SCENARIO = _batch_config["BASELINE_BILL_SCENARIO"]

# Heating season for the winter-only charts: Oct–Mar.
WINTER_MONTHS = ["Oct", "Nov", "Dec", "Jan", "Feb", "Mar"]

print(f"state={STATE}  batch={BATCH}  utility={UTILITY}  scenario={DEFAULT_SCENARIO}  bill_col={BILL_COL}")
```

Every bill-change comparison below reads the `BILL_COL` column set above — currently
**`{python} BILL_COL`**. Leaving it at `energy_total_bill` compares baseline (undiscounted)
bills; switching it to `energy_total_bill_lmi_48` or `energy_total_bill_lmi_100` reruns every
comparison net of Maryland's OHEP low-income bill discount, at 48% or 100% participation
respectively.

`segment_name()` turns a scenario + stage into the directory name CAIRO's post-processing
writes master tables under:

- **`precalc`** — today's mixed heating population (pre-retrofit), Schedule R as filed. This
  is our **baseline**: `default_r_uncalibrated_precalc/`.
- **`calibrated`** — the same buildings retrofitted to a heat pump, still on Schedule R as
  filed. This is our **after**: `default_r_uncalibrated_calibrated/`.

```{python}
#| label: ingest

SEG_DEFAULT_PRECALC = segment_name(DEFAULT_SCENARIO, "precalc")
SEG_DEFAULT_CALIBRATED = segment_name(DEFAULT_SCENARIO, "calibrated")

bills_default_precalc = load_master_bills(STATE, BATCH, SEG_DEFAULT_PRECALC)
bills_default_calibrated = load_master_bills(STATE, BATCH, SEG_DEFAULT_CALIBRATED)

print(f"baseline segment: {SEG_DEFAULT_PRECALC}")
print(f"after segment:    {SEG_DEFAULT_CALIBRATED}")
```

Let's look at a sample of the baseline bills to see what's in the table, and check the sample
size — how many ResStock buildings we have, and how many actual MD BGE residential customers
they represent once we sum ResStock's sample weights.

```{python}
#| label: sample-size

_sample = cast(
    pl.DataFrame,
    bills_default_precalc
    .filter(pl.col("month") == "Annual")
    .select("bldg_id", "weight", "postprocess_group.heating_type_v2", "postprocess_group.has_hp", "energy_total_bill")
    .collect(),
)
print(_sample.head())

n_resstock_bldgs = _sample["bldg_id"].n_unique()
n_utility_customers = float(_sample["weight"].sum())
report_vars["n_resstock_bldgs"] = n_resstock_bldgs
report_vars["n_utility_customers"] = n_utility_customers
print(f"Unique ResStock buildings: {n_resstock_bldgs:,}")
print(f"Total MD BGE residential customers (sum of weights): {n_utility_customers:,.0f}")
```

## Bill-increase incidence switching from natural gas to a heat pump, under Schedule R

How often does a natural-gas-heated MD BGE home end up with a *higher* total annual energy
bill (electric + gas) after switching to a heat pump, if nothing about the rate design
changes? We diff each building's annual **`{python} BILL_COL`** between
`default_r_uncalibrated_precalc` (today's HVAC, Schedule R as filed) and
`default_r_uncalibrated_calibrated` (same building retrofitted to a heat pump, same tariff)
— a same-scenario, before/after-retrofit comparison — restricted to buildings whose baseline
heating fuel is natural gas.

```{python}
#| label: compute-natgas-hp-delta-default

delta_natgas_default = bill_delta_between_segments(
    STATE, BATCH, SEG_DEFAULT_PRECALC, SEG_DEFAULT_CALIBRATED, bill_col=BILL_COL
).filter(pl.col("heating_type_v2") == "natgas")

incidence_natgas_default = bill_change_incidence(delta_natgas_default)
incidence_natgas_default
```

```{python}
#| label: report-vars-natgas-hp-delta-default

report_vars["pct_natgas_hp_bill_increase_default"] = incidence_natgas_default["pct_increase"]
report_vars["pct_natgas_hp_bill_decrease_default"] = incidence_natgas_default["pct_decrease"]
report_vars["mean_natgas_hp_bill_increase_default"] = incidence_natgas_default["mean_delta"]
report_vars["median_natgas_hp_bill_increase_default"] = incidence_natgas_default["median_delta"]
```

**`{python} f"{report_vars['pct_natgas_hp_bill_increase_default']:.0%}"` of natural-gas-heated
MD BGE homes would see their total annual energy bill go up** after switching to a heat pump
under Schedule R as filed — a mean increase of
`{python} f"${report_vars['mean_natgas_hp_bill_increase_default']:,.0f}"` a year (median
`{python} f"${report_vars['median_natgas_hp_bill_increase_default']:,.0f}"`). The rest see a
decrease, mostly from avoided gas costs outweighing the added electric load.

## Bill change quadrant plot

`plot_bill_change_quadrants()` gives a more granular view of the same before/after-retrofit
comparison — instead of just a mean and median, it shows the weighted share of households
landing in each of four savings/loss bins ($0-1k and >$1k, in each direction), split by
baseline heating type.

```{python}
#| label: fig-bill-change-quadrants-default-all
#| fig-cap: "Change in total annual energy bill after switching to a heat pump, by baseline heating type, under MD BGE's Schedule R (as filed)."

plot_bill_change_quadrants(
    STATE, BATCH, SEG_DEFAULT_PRECALC, SEG_DEFAULT_CALIBRATED,
    bill_col=BILL_COL,
    rate_name="Schedule R rate (as filed)",
)
```

The annual view mixes summer cooling with winter heating. Restricting the same before/after-retrofit comparison to October–March isolates the months where a heat pump actually replaces the furnace. The `$1k` bins are still absolute dollars over those six months, not a scaled annual equivalent.

```{python}
#| label: fig-bill-change-quadrants-default-winter
#| fig-cap: "Change in total Oct–March energy bill after switching to a heat pump, by baseline heating type, under MD BGE's Schedule R (as filed)."

plot_bill_change_quadrants(
    STATE, BATCH, SEG_DEFAULT_PRECALC, SEG_DEFAULT_CALIBRATED,
    bill_col=BILL_COL,
    rate_name="Schedule R rate (as filed)",
    month=WINTER_MONTHS,
)
```

The stacked bars above compress each heating type into four bins; the histogram below shows
the full weighted distribution for natural-gas-heated homes only, under the same
before/after-retrofit comparison.

```{python}
#| label: fig-hist-natgas-bill-change-default
#| fig-cap: "Distribution of the annual total energy bill change for natural-gas-heated MD BGE homes after switching to a heat pump, under Schedule R as filed."

plot_weighted_bill_change_hist(
    delta_natgas_default,
    "Natural-gas homes switching to a heat pump under Schedule R (as filed)",
)
```

Restricting to just the natural-gas subclass isolates the incidence figure computed above
(`{python} f"{report_vars['pct_natgas_hp_bill_increase_default']:.0%}"` seeing an increase)
into the same savings/loss bins, rather than just a binary increase/decrease split.

## Export report variables

This notebook writes to its own cache file (`bills_only_report_variables.pkl`), separate from
`analysis.qmd`'s `report_variables.pkl`, since both are rendered in the same Quarto project
and a shared, fully-overwritten cache file would let whichever notebook renders last silently
clobber the other's variables.

```{python}
#| label: export-report-vars

import pickle

Path("../cache").mkdir(exist_ok=True)
Path("../cache/bills_only_report_variables.pkl").write_bytes(pickle.dumps(report_vars))
report_vars
```
